title: The Woman Who Stayed
passages:
At eleven-oh-eight the ebb leaned hard against the Marrow's stern, and Rusk's dead barge had to swing clear or take the turn broadside and stove itself on the customs-house columns. Bayo took the wheel. Sol stayed at his shoulder with her hands on the spoke-box, watching him like she expected him to bolt.

Salas stood aft by the winch drum, one hand on the brake, his coat dripping salt water. He had risen off the drum when the bell rang, and he watched Bayo with full awareness of their history, confirming Bayo's face showed no change.

"True line," Bayo said. He killed the auxiliary and let the current yaw them. "Off the columns, not his poles. Rusk's markers are forty meters wrong, and he knows it."

"Then why's he still holding the mouth?" Sol said.

"Because he's patient," Bayo said. "And because he's got nothing else to do but wait for us to come up heavy." He eased the throttle. The Marrow's screws bit water, and the boat slid forward, close enough that Sol could see the rust scored into the ferry ribs jutting from the channel wall. Rusk's barge groaned, its cables singing as it pivoted on the lanyard, swinging its broad stern away from the gap just before the ebb could catch it and pin it against the drowned span.

Rusk's voice carried from the water, thin but clear: "Settle back, then. I'll sit right here."

Bayo didn't answer. He held the wheel steady while the Marrow threaded the gap, the columns sliding past on either side close enough to touch the ferry ribs. Sol kept her breath even, not touching the wheel.

"Through," Bayo said.

Sol let out the breath she'd been holding. "Rusk said he'd wait."

"He will," Bayo said. "Right up until he decides he won't."

The barge settled back across the channel mouth behind them, Rusk still in the water at its port side, lanyard taken up on his arm, holding the Stair shut while his arm rested. He called after them, voice rising over the water: "I'll be here when you come up heavy."

Sol turned to the compass box and set course for Mercy General's drowned flank. The bell had rung two notes. Mara was waiting, or whatever was left of her. And the season bell would seal the channel before they could run back out.

"Full ahead," Sol said.

Bayo's hands stayed on the wheel. "Aye, Captain."

Sol didn't look at him. She had heard him make that promise before.
